Bitcoin’s Post-Quantum Solutions

Bitcoin’s Post-Quantum Solutions

October 14, 2026
26 min read

By: David Puell

Research Trading Analyst/Associate Portfolio Manager, Digital Assets

More from David Puell

Join the conversation

As Digital Assets Trading Analyst, David focuses on Bitcoin and cryptoasset on-chain and market research.

Introduction: Bitcoin’s “Q-Day” Has Been Front-Page NewsQuantum computing has become a hot topic in the Bitcoin ecosystem. In March, Google Quantum AI and Oratomic/Caltech published whitepapers within hours of each other, each restating the resource estimates for breaking the cryptographic signature schemes that underlie property rights in the Bitcoin network. Each compressed the resources necessary to run Shor's algorithm and break Bitcoin’s 256-bit Elliptic-Curve Cryptography (ECC-256). That milestone has shifted the quantum threat from "decades away" to "within a decade, possibly."Most ordinary Bitcoin spends today ultimately rely on secp256k1 elliptic-curve signatures. What does that mean? Bitcoin uses Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC)—specifically called secp256k1—a 256-bit elliptic curve that generates the public-private key pairs securing every wallet. Deriving the private key from the public key is not feasible computationally—at least on a classical computer. The underlying one-way problem is called the Elliptic Curve Discrete Logarithm Problem (ECDLP).Per WickedSmartBitcoin.com, approximately 35% of bitcoin’s (BTC’s) total supply is secured only by elliptic curve digital signatures. Per Project Eleven, the same is true for roughly two-thirds of ether (ETH) and 100% of solana (SOL). The remaining supplies are protected because their public keys are hidden from potential attackers.“Q-Day” is the hypothetical date on which a cryptographically-relevant quantum computer (CRQC) will be able to break ECC-256 in relevant timeframes—fast enough, that is, to compromise real transactions or expose dormant bitcoin before the network can respond. Shor’s algorithm is the mechanism by which that break can occur, as it can solve the ECDLP exponentially faster than any known classical algorithm, reducing the private key derivation problem from billions of years to days, hours, or even minutes—assuming a sufficiently capable fault-tolerant quantum computer.What Quantum Can And Cannot BreakQuantum Algorithms: Shor’s And Grover’sWidely known as the “big two” quantum computing algorithms, Shor’s and Grover’s would subject the Bitcoin protocol to significantly different risk profiles.Shor’s algorithm uses quantum period-finding to solve the ECDLP exponentially faster than classical computers. In other words, a sufficiently large quantum computer could derive a bitcoin private key from an exposed public key and break the security assumption underlying ECC-256 signatures that secure coin ownership. Less potent a force, Grover’s algorithm offers a quadratic speedup for brute-force search, halving the strength of bitcoin's SHA-256 hashing (256-bit to 128-bit security)—weakening instead of breaking the security, which we believe the network's design would be able to absorb comfortably. Quantum attackers would have to compete with the robust and highly specialized classical application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs) in Bitcoin mining machines. In short, Shor's algorithm is the real long-term threat.Note: Shor's exponential speedup fully breaks elliptic-curve signatures, while Grover's quadratic speedup only halves hash security - a margin bitcoin's 256-bit primitives were designed to absorb. Source: ARK Investment Management LLC, 2026. For informational purposes only and should not be considered investment advice or a recommendation to buy, sell, or hold any particular security or cryptocurrency.Two Types Of Shor’s Attack: Short-Range And Long-RangeShor’s algorithm can attack Bitcoin in two ways, their distinction reflecting one variable: time. Bitcoin's rough 10-minute block time is the threshold that separates the two types of attack. A short-range attack would race the clock, cracking a key from the mempool1 and front-running a live transaction before the next block confirms. Because most conventional transactions are transparent the moment a coin moves, no public key address hygiene could protect an in-flight transaction. In this scenario, spending would become unsafe and, in our view, the network could collapse. A long-range attack would face no deadline, which implies less short-term risk but more time for the attack: public keys already sitting on-chain in pay-to-public-key (P2PK) outputs and reused addresses—roughly 35% of bitcoin's supply, including approximately 1.1 million Satoshi-era coins—could be harvested over weeks or months.Note: Qubit estimates carry wide uncertainty. Source: ARK Investment Management LLC, 2026. For informational purposes only and should not be considered investment advice or a recommendation to buy, sell, or hold any particular security or cryptocurrency.Critically, the hardware requirements for the two attacks are orders of magnitude different. Beating the 10-minute clock demands the nanosecond gate speeds of superconducting or photonic architectures—which we believe will be slower to scale to cryptographically relevant size. The long-range attack, in contrast, could run on any fault-tolerant platform, including neutral atoms—where uncharged atoms are held in laser “tweezer” arrays, as the electron’s grounded or excited state serves as the qubit—which are scaling quicker. In other words, the long-range attack is likely to be feasible first, a reason we believe that the short-term solutions are more behavioral: migrating coins to fresh, hashed addresses, and coordinating a post-quantum signature upgrade before a quantum hardware is viable. Neither solution is trivial. Post-quantum signatures could be 10–780x larger than those today and would strain block space, while coins in wallets with lost keys would not be able to migrate at all, forcing the network to confront a critical governance decision: whether to freeze vulnerable outputs or to leave them as bounty for a quantum attacker.Protocol-Level SolutionsWith the publication of the Google AI and Oratomic/Caltech papers, several post-quantum bitcoin solutions have emerged or re-emerged. Below, we provide an overview of those solutions.The Bitcoin Improvement Proposal 360 (BIP-360) The first sign that Bitcoin developers are taking the quantum threat seriously is BIP-360, a soft-fork draft proposal merged into the official BIP repository in February 2026. Repository inclusion means that developers have documented the proposal formally but does not mean that Bitcoin Core or the network has adopted it. BIP-360 introduces Pay-to-Merkle-Root (P2MR), a Taproot-like script-tree output without the quantum-vulnerable key-path spend. Properly constructed, P2MR outputs would resist long-exposure attacks and provide a clean container for future signature operations. That said, BIP-360 does not add or select a post-quantum signature scheme or protect ordinary elliptic-curve spends from short-exposure attacks.HashesThe most conservative option for Bitcoin security, hash-based signatures, ask Bitcoin developers to trust new math the least. Their security is dependent on hash functions like SHA-256, the battle-tested primitive that already secures bitcoin mining. Instead of relying on elliptic curves threatened by a quantum computer, the signer proves ownership by revealing private values that match previously published hashes. In 2024, the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) blessed this approach when it standardized SPHINCS+ as SLH-DSA—a hash-based signature scheme aligned with Bitcoin’s risk-averse cryptographic standards yet heavy at 8,000-50,000 bytes. Evidently, the tradeoff is size: up to 120-780 times larger than Bitcoin's current signatures, potentially straining both block space and transaction throughput.Specialized research is exploring smaller tradeoffs. In December 2025, Blockstream Research introduced SHRINCS, which combines a compact stateful signing path with a larger stateless fallback. In early days, it advertised signatures as small as 324 bytes, and within five months a May 2026 Bitcoin opcode sketch modeled a 580-byte compact path. BIP-360 also discusses future script upgrades that could support one-time signatures like Lamport and Winternitz, though those designs impose strict key-reuse constraints.LatticesIf hash-based signatures are the safe route to security, lattice-based signatures are the practical ones. They rely on a newer branch of mathematics—finding hidden points in vast, high-dimensional grids—that even quantum computers seem so far unable to crack. Their appeal is efficiency: signatures measured in hundreds or low thousands of bytes, not tens of thousands, with rapid verification. In 2022, NIST standardized ML-DSA and selected Falcon—now standardizing as FN-DSA—as a potential standard. ML-DSA signatures range from ~2.4 to ~4.6 kilobytes. Falcon-512’s commonly cited padded signature is ~666 bytes, ~10 times the size of a Bitcoin Schnorr signature. The tradeoff is historical proof: lattice problems have been studied for decades, though much less than hash functions. As a result, the risk of an unexpected mathematical break, while low, is not zero. Although earlier versions of BIP-360 evaluated post-quantum algorithms, the current proposal leaves signature selection to a future consensus proposal.IsogenyIsogeny-based cryptography is the high-risk, high-reward candidate in the field. Its math—mapping relationships among special elliptic curves—produces remarkably small keys and signatures, which would be very well suited to a block-space-constrained network like Bitcoin, except for a historical scar. In 2022, researchers broke SIDH/SIKE, then a leading isogeny scheme in NIST's competition, in roughly one hour using, not a quantum computer, but an ordinary classical computer. In May 2026, SQIsign advanced to the third round of NIST’s additional-signature competition after an early version of BIP-360 removed it in January 2025 based on performance concerns. SQIsign implementations have improved substantially since then, but the current direction of Bitcoin research suggests that near-term deployment of isogeny-based signatures is unlikely.HybridsHybrid schemes answer a simple question: what if the new cryptography is flawed? The solution would be two locks on every coin—one classical (today's ECDSA or Schnorr signatures) and one post-quantum—so that an attacker must break both. This hybrid approach is already mainstream for internet keys. By default, Chrome combines classical X25519 with post-quantum ML-KEM for Transport Layer Security (TLS) connections—the protocol that encrypts data between a device and a server. According to Cloudflare, this double-lock traffic increased from under 3% in early 2024 to over 65% of its human-generated TLS traffic in April 2026. While these deployments involve hybrid key exchange instead of hybrid digital signatures, they incorporate the same risk-management. The cost here is obvious: two signatures take up more space than one.Modular SolutionsInstead of betting on one algorithm, modular designs rebuild Bitcoin so that its signature schemes can swap out over time—equivalent to designing a house with replaceable locks instead of doors welded shut. The SegWit upgrade in 2017 and Taproot in 2021 both reserved room for such rule changes. BIP-360 extends this logic by keeping public keys hidden until the moment coins are spent, creating a framework in which multiple quantum-resistant algorithms can coexist. Future algorithms can be added without replacing the output type again, although each new consensus-level signature rule would require network review and activation. The cost of this future-proofing is more complexity for wallets and developers, not to mention the challenge of finding consensus within a decentralized network.Commit-Delay-Reveal SchemesThese protocols tackle the nightmare scenario: quantum computers hitting prime time before bitcoin holders have moved their coins. Commit-delay-reveal enables a bitcoin holder to migrate safely. First, owners publish cryptographic commitments—sealed envelopes proving they intend to move specific coins without revealing the crucial public key to a quantum attacker. After a mandatory waiting period, they open the envelopes and spend. Cracking the key at that point would be too late, since only someone with prior knowledge of the key could have posted the earlier commitment. MIT-affiliated developer Tadge Dryja's 2025 "Lifeboat" proposal offers a modern version deployable as a soft fork. This proposal also has limits: long waits, more complexity, and no protection for the roughly 35% of supply with public keys already exposed on-chain.Lost-Coins SolutionsWe know that ~35% of bitcoin supply is vulnerable to the potential of quantum computing’s long-range attacks. Most of those coins can be moved safely to secure addresses today by following best practices, primarily migrating them to non-reused addresses with hidden public keys. A large share of exposed supply—about 1.6–1.8 million BTC—sits with exchanges and some custodians, such as Binance (~83–85% of its balance exposed) and Robinhood (100%). That said, even if major exchanges adjust to post-quantum standards over time, ~8% to 12% of total supply—largely assumed lost and inaccessible—would be exposed to quantum theft indefinitely.The Lost-Coins TrilemmaThe fate of “lost” bitcoin could be the most crucial debate in the history of Bitcoin. Today, the debate has formed around a trilemma: if quantum-capable actors can spend coins that their original owners cannot spend, Bitcoin will violate various rights:Doing nothing violates property rights: Leaving old scripts valid, and lost coins unprotected, preserves historical consensus rules but enables a new actor to redistribute dormant supply without property rights.Freezing the lost coins violates immutability: Freezing the coins preserves the economic status quo but invalidates spending conditions once considered final.Straddling those two choices creates an imbalance between property rights and immutability: Throttling attempts to timestamp the freezing of lost coins over months or years aims for procedural neutrality but harms validation and delays the redistribution. Recovery proofs can soften the trilemma, but they cannot recover every abandoned coin.The trilemma remains debated among the bitcoin community and will likely become increasingly contentious.Alternative Solutions For Unretrievable CoinsApart from the three options described above, alternative solutions have been proposed or theorized:Recycling of coins into the security budget: Instead of letting recovered coins hit the market and impact price, meter them back into the ecosystem as future mining rewards, converting a stranded liability into a "second subsidy" that shores up bitcoin's long-term security—as block rewards decay with every halving. As of today, no mature Bitcoin proposal includes this option.Nic Carter's salvage-in-trust: A government-appointed entity or licensed lab uses a quantum computer to "salvage" the vulnerable coins and hold them in trust for the original owners. This approach was inspired by maritime salvage law, in which the salvor may earn, hypothetically, a 10–15% fee, while rightful owners like Satoshi Nakamoto can reclaim their coins anytime and unclaimed coins eventually revert to the state, avoiding any change to the protocol itself.Zero-knowledge proof-of-ownership recovery: Owners unlock otherwise-stranded coins by proving knowledge of their BIP-39 seed phrase with a ZK proof, demonstrating legitimate ownership without exposing the quantum-vulnerable public key.Sanctioned white-hat recovery: Researchers have outlined a "quantum recovery tool" that would recover vulnerable coins proactively before adversarial quantum computers mature—a coordinated, defensive race to sweep exposed coins into safe custody rather than exposing them to the first attack, though its technical feasibility still is in question.Block Space Traffic Jam?Bitcoin's block space is a fixed constraint, within which the migration away from quantum-vulnerable cryptography must fit. WickedSmartBitcoin.com estimates that moving the ~35% of supply exposed to a long-range attack would take ~141 days and ~20 thousand blocks. Unfortunately, every byte devoted to such a migration would bid up fees and congest the network, impacting ordinary users.The severity of the traffic jam would be a function of one variable: time. In our view, the cost of migration is not fixed. With procrastination come penalties. The earlier the network commits to a migration path, the lower the toll per block.Timeline And Hurdles Of Potential SolutionsWhat We Can Do TodayThe highest-return work requires no network-wide agreement at all and can start now. Custodians, exchanges, funds, miners, and individual holders can put their own houses in order:Take inventory: Sort holdings by how exposed they are. Coins with public keys are visible on-chain and most at risk.Practice good key hygiene and adopt best practices: Stop reusing addresses, move coins away from keys that have been surfaced, and share extended public keys and wallet descriptors only when necessary.Preserve a paper trail: Keep seed phrases, derivation paths, and records of the genesis of each wallet. That important documentation can prove ownership in the future.Map out mobility: Institutions should go one step further and map which coins can move: some are locked by contracts, some by timelocks, some dependent on third-party signers.Together, these steps will convert an opaque balance into a prioritized migration queue.What Requires ConsensusSome decisions cannot be made by individuals and require consensus among the Bitcoin developers. In our view, protocol consensus efforts should focus on solutions to four pressing matters in the following order:A safer output type—such as Pay-to-Merkle-Root (P2MR)—that keeps public keys hidden while coins are at rest and provides an upgrade path for later post-quantum signature rules.One or more quantum-resistant signature methods that the network will accept as valid proof of ownership and new property rights.Perhaps review accounting rules for block space, so that larger post-quantum signatures don't slow verification or expose the network to spam and denial-of-service attacks.An activation plan for coins left in legacy addresses when the new rules are put in place.The sequencing will be critical: the network can ship the new address type first, creating a safe container for migrating coins, before settling the more difficult debate over the signature scheme that will become permanent.What We Can Do After ActivationOnce the upgrade activates, no one will direct the migration. Bitcoin has no authority to decide who moves first. In a rush, everyone will try to do so at the same time. The realistic order will be set by the fee market, giving those willing to pay more the ability to migrate first. To prevent a stampede, the goal is not centralized coordination but a longer runway and lower tolls. Simply put:Start early and migrate slowly. The best defense against a fee-based stampede is time. A migration years before quantum computers debut will require a small share of each block, as opposed to one that begins after the first credible attack, which will be a race to the bottom.Make the least expensive path the default. Wallet providers should be able to default every new address to the quantum-safe type so that ordinary users migrate passively by transacting and avoid paying a premium on panic.Batch for everyone, not just the big institutions. When exchanges and custodians consolidate transfers, they can migrate millions of customer balances—including small ones—in a fraction of the block space that individual transactions otherwise would consume. Self-custodied holders benefit too, as batching frees capacity for everyone.Consider protocol-level incentives. The network could offer discounts for migration transactions in its block-space accounting—as SegWit once did for witness data—making the safe move the affordable move, regardless of wallet size.Conclusion: The Top Priority Is Network SecurityGiven the pace of development in AI and quantum computing, security could be the most important challenge for bitcoin holders, institutions, and other market participants. Shor's algorithm poses an existential threat to the signatures securing roughly 35% of bitcoin's supply. A long-range attack on exposed keys will become feasible and necessary well before any attacker can outrun the 10-minute clock on live transactions.Cryptographic tools—hash-based schemes, lattices, hybrids, and modular designs—are maturing rapidly. The cost of migration is not fixed by technical constraints but a penalty for procrastination: begun early, migration is absorbed at the margin into each block but, delayed, it becomes a race to limit the loss.In our view, Bitcoin's quantum transition is less a question of the technology than the network's governance. Will the Bitcoin network prepare the ecosystem early enough? The networks, institutions, and holders that treat security as a strategy instead of an afterthought will define the next chapter of sound digital money. In that race, the clock favors the prepared. At ARK, we know that innovation solves problems. Now is the time to innovate.Important InformationBitcoin is a relatively new asset class, and the market for bitcoin is subject to rapid changes and uncertainty. Bitcoin is largely unregulated and bitcoin investments may be more susceptible to fraud and manipulation than more regulated investments. Bitcoin is subject to unique and substantial risks, including significant price volatility and lack of liquidity, and theft.Bitcoin is subject to rapid price swings, including as a result of actions and statements by influencers and the media, changes in the supply of and demand for bitcoin, and other factors. There is no assurance that bitcoin will maintain its value over the long term. ARK strongly encourages any investor considering an investment in bitcoin or any other digital asset to consult with a financial professional before investing.

1

Mempool: Short for “memory pool,” it is a node's holding area in the Bitcoin network for valid but unconfirmed transactions that are waiting to be included in the next block by a miner.
